title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
formal: Does there exist a single deterministic classical Turing algorithm that, for every valid finite description of a memoryless finite-dimensional quantum channel \(\Phi\) specified below and every positive rational \(\varepsilon\), halts and outputs a rational \(r\) satisfying \(|r-Q(\Phi)|\le\varepsilon\)? Here \(Q\) is unassisted, vanishing-error quantum capacity in qubits per channel use. The algorithm must work for all valid descriptions and all positive requested accuracies; there is no time or space bound beyond eventual halting.
definitions:
The input consists of positive integers \(d_A,d_B\), a finite program \(P\) for an ordinary deterministic Turing machine, and a positive rational \(\varepsilon\). Integers use binary notation and a rational uses a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. Programs use one fixed effective encoding over a finite alphabet; choosing a different standard encoding only changes effective translations. Write \(A=\mathbb C^{d_A}\), \(B=\mathbb C^{d_B}\). The program \(P\), on every positive integer input \(m\), is promised to halt and output a complex matrix \(J_m\) of order \(d_Ad_B\), with rational real and imaginary entries in this encoding. There is a matrix \(J\) such that, for every entry, both its real and imaginary parts differ from those of \(J_m\) by at most \(2^{-m}\). No additional time bound on \(P\) is promised. The approximating matrices themselves need not be positive or trace preserving.

Index matrix entries by pairs \((i,u)\), with \(1\le i\le d_A\) and \(1\le u\le d_B\). The limiting matrix is promised to be positive semidefinite and to satisfy \[\sum_{u=1}^{d_B}J_{(i,u),(j,u)}=\delta_{ij}\qquad(1\le i,j\le d_A),\] where \(\delta_{ij}\) is one if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. These conditions say \(\operatorname{Tr}_B J=I_A\). They make \(J\) the unnormalized Choi matrix of the unique CPTP channel defined on matrix units by \([\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)]_{u,v}=J_{(i,u),(j,v)}\) and extended complex-linearly. Equivalently, \(J=\sum_{i,j}|i\rangle\langle j|\otimes\Phi(|i\rangle\langle j|)\). The guarantee supplies effective approximation of arbitrary computable complex entries; algebraic-entry channels and ordinary finite circuits over computable gates are included. The algorithm receives the program's finite code and may execute it. It receives no oracle deciding equality, positivity or ordering of arbitrary computable real numbers.

All guarantees for the requested capacity algorithm apply only to inputs satisfying these promises. It need not recognize validity and has no prescribed behavior on invalid descriptions. Every valid program describing the same channel must yield an approximation to that channel's same capacity, though the output rational and running time may differ between programs. The description specifies the channel, not a particular encoder or decoder.

A density matrix on \(\mathbb C^d\) is a Hermitian matrix \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\) satisfying \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A quantum channel from \(\mathbb C^a\) to \(\mathbb C^b\) is a complex-linear map on matrices of the form \(\Psi(X)=\sum_j K_jXK_j^\dagger\), with finitely many \(b\)-by-\(a\) matrices obeying \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I_a\). These are precisely the completely positive trace-preserving maps, abbreviated CPTP. Matrices in coding operations may have arbitrary complex entries. Memorylessness means that \(n\) uses of a fixed channel \(\Phi:A\to B\) act as the tensor power \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\), with independent noise and the same channel on every use.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), a code consists of a nonnegative integer \(k_n\), a CPTP encoder \(E_n\) from \(k_n\) qubits to \(A^{\otimes n}\), and a CPTP decoder \(D_n\) from \(B^{\otimes n}\) to \(k_n\) qubits. A qubit is a copy of \(\mathbb C^2\), so the message space has dimension \(2^{k_n}\). Let \[|\Omega_k\rangle=2^{-k/2}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle_R\otimes|x\rangle_M\] be a maximally entangled unit vector between an untouched reference register \(R\) and a message register \(M\), each of dimension \(2^k\). For \(k=0\), both spaces are one-dimensional and the sum has one term. The entanglement fidelity of a code is \[F_n=\langle\Omega_{k_n}|\bigl[\operatorname{id}_R\otimes(D_n\circ\Phi^{\otimes n}\circ E_n)\bigr](|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle\langle\Omega_{k_n}|)|\Omega_{k_n}\rangle.\] The identity map leaves the reference unchanged, and \(\circ\) denotes composition, with the rightmost operation applied first. This tests preservation of quantum information and its correlations, rather than only classical basis labels.

A real rate \(r\ge0\) is achievable if there is a sequence of these codes, one for every \(n\ge1\), such that \(F_n\to1\) and \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}k_n/n\ge r\). Define \(Q(\Phi)\) as the supremum of achievable rates, in qubits per channel use. Rate zero is always achievable. The encoder and decoder may jointly process their entire blocks, use local ancillary systems and discard local systems. There is no bound on their computation or circuit sizes and no uniformity requirement on the sequence of codes. They depend on the channel but not on the unknown input message state. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary quantum channel is supplied. The reference in the fidelity test is a mathematical test system, not a communication resource. The whole coding map is trace preserving: postselecting a successful event for free is not allowed. This is asymptotic, vanishing-error, unassisted quantum transmission capacity.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of such an algorithm, including its termination and additive error guarantee for every valid description and every positive rational \(\varepsilon\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such single algorithm exists in the specified input representation. The negative alternative means that every candidate algorithm fails termination or the error guarantee on at least one promised input and requested accuracy. The yes/no assertion quantifies over all requested accuracies; a fixed \(1/100\) error guarantee is not a replacement for it. A regularized formula without a finite stopping guarantee, polynomial-time hardness, or undecidability for an assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity does not answer this question. Nor would undecidability of the exact predicate \(Q(\Phi)=0\) alone rule out additive approximation.
why: Determine whether the fundamental reliable quantum communication rate is algorithmically accessible even without efficiency constraints.

importance.reason: A foundational computability question about regularized information quantities, separating lack of efficient algorithms from the possible absence of any certified approximation algorithm.

progress.text: Devetak proves a quantum coding theorem yielding the regularized coherent-information expression for unassisted capacity.
Leung–Smith establish explicit continuity bounds for finite-dimensional unassisted quantum capacity.
Cubitt and coauthors prove that arbitrarily many channel uses may be needed before positive coherent information appears.
Undecidability in Physics reviews the open computability issue and distinguishes memoryful channels and zero-error capacities.

Bhattacharyya–Mehta–Zhao’s corrected v3 proves circuit-input QMA-hardness for quantum capacity and undecidability for a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity; ordinary quantum-capacity computability remains open.

status_note: Source-open. On 16 September 2026 selected full primary statements on coding, continuity, unbounded block lengths and the 2025 review were checked, together with the corrected March 2026 paper, its current revision metadata and bounded later-work searches. The 2026 paper explicitly leaves general quantum-capacity computability open. Its QMA-hardness is for succinct circuit input; its undecidability result concerns a restricted entanglement-assisted one-shot zero-error classical capacity. Neither resolves the retained uniform approximation question. No cited proof was independently verified or formalized in Lean.

context_blocks.text: Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem identifies the operational capacity with \(\sup_{n\ge1} n^{-1}\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi^{\otimes n})\). Here \(\rho\) ranges over all input density matrices on \(A^{\otimes n}\). If \(|\psi\rangle\) is a purification of \(\rho\), meaning a unit vector on a reference and the input with input marginal \(\rho\), and \(\omega=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi^{\otimes n})(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\), then \(I_c=S(\omega_{B^{\otimes n}})-S(\omega)\). The marginal is obtained by tracing out the reference. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of a density matrix, \(S=-\sum_j\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\). The result is independent of the chosen purification. This exact regularized expression includes every block length; it is not an evaluation of the capacity curve or a finite stopping rule.

The regularized formula gives approximable finite-dimensional objectives at every fixed block length. This yields lower semicomputability: certified rational lower bounds can approach capacity. Such a sequence alone need not tell an algorithm when its distance from the limit is below a requested tolerance.

Cubitt and coauthors prove that no fixed number of channel uses suffices uniformly over all channels even to detect positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there but whose capacity is positive. The channel can change with the chosen length. This does not rule out an algorithm with stopping time depending on the channel description and requested accuracy.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least \(3/4\) from capacity at most \(1/4\), even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.

sentences: Quantum channel capacity describes the best asymptotic rate for transmitting quantum information through a noisy channel.
This problem asks whether that number can always be approximated by an algorithm from an effective finite description of the channel.
The algorithm may be slow, but it must halt and meet any requested rational accuracy.
Optimizations involving arbitrarily many channel uses make the asymptotic definition harder to turn into a guaranteed finite computation.
Establishing computability or an obstruction would separate the existence of an operational communication rate from our ability to calculate it even in principle.
